overview: This imported label needs a map warning. Its 1500 to 500 BCE outline consists of disconnected areas in Sinai and eastern Iraq/western Iran, excluding the Syrian centers of the Aramaean kingdoms. It cannot be read as one empire or one people. This card therefore separates regional archaeology from the Aramaean states named in the label; each example identifies its own place and period.

periods.title: Sinai within an older mining world
periods.summary: The earlier map window overlaps Egyptian New Kingdom mining connections; it is not an Aramaean founding date.

periods.title: Separate Iron Age centers
periods.summary: Small Syrian and Anatolian kingdoms flourished alongside distinct Iranian settlements. No ruler united these examples.

periods.title: Conquests and wider use of Aramaic
periods.summary: Aramaean kingdoms lost independence under Assyria; their writing continued into Persian administration.

items.text: After the Hittite imperial collapse around 1180 BCE, small states developed in southern Anatolia and Syria. Tell Tayinat and Sam’al had their own courts. Archaeologists distinguish Aramaean and Neo-Hittite traditions, although local histories intersected. Assyria was a separate expanding empire, not another name for this network.

At Tell Tayinat in the Amuq plain, excavators uncovered palaces with columned entrances, temples and monumental gateways. This was the capital of Patina, a regional kingdom. Its conquest by Assyria in 738 BCE is one documented political ending, not a fall date for every Aramaean-speaking community.

At Sam’al, now Zincirli in Türkiye, King Bar-Rakib’s late eighth-century BCE palace inscription proclaims loyalty to the Assyrian king and names his royal father. A handsome new palace could advertise both family legitimacy and dependence on a stronger neighbor.

A ninth-century BCE stele from Brej, north of Aleppo, supplies a short Aramaic sample: mlk ʾrm, “king of Aram.” This is a modern scholarly transliteration of line 3, not modern words invented for the card. The inscription dedicates a monument to Melqart; it was found outside the highlighted polygons.

Aramaic scribes used an alphabet of 22 consonantal signs. Court inscriptions and faster cursive writing developed different letter shapes. Stone monuments preserve part of this skilled work, but royal literacy should not be mistaken for evidence that every child attended school.

sections.title: Sinai: stone, work and royal expeditions

items.text: In southwestern Sinai, Wadi Maghara and Serabit el-Khadim supplied turquoise. Mining tools, tool-making installations, habitation remains and inscriptions document organized expeditions during the third and second millennia BCE. The mines had a long history before this map begins. Their blue-green stone traveled into Egyptian beads, amulets and jewelry inlays.

A blue-green jewel was not necessarily turquoise. New Kingdom and Third Intermediate Period ornaments also used opaque glass and faience. Museum scientists now compare elemental signatures with X-ray fluorescence to distinguish materials and help trace sources without cutting out a sample. Ancient craft and modern chemistry make a good detective team.

A thirteenth-century BCE statue of Ramesses II from Serabit el-Khadim includes his daughter Bintanat on its left side. Its inscriptions connect the king with Hathor and turquoise. This is a named royal family presented at a mining sanctuary, showing how resource expeditions, religious devotion and royal images could meet in one place.

sections.title: Western Iran: homes, tools and meals

items.text: Hasanlu, near Lake Urmia in northwestern Iran, stood on routes linking the Zagros with Anatolia and Mesopotamia. Its early Iron Age workshops and rich finds reveal a substantial local center. No preserved local written language securely identifies its inhabitants, so its position within an atlas polygon does not make them Aramaeans.

In Hasanlu’s Iron Age residential Building III, a columned hall had a central hearth, wall benches, adjacent kitchens and storerooms. Stairs reached an upper floor. This substantial household had rooms for cooking, storage and gathering, rather than one empty hall devoted only to a ruler’s throne.

Hasanlu’s excavated pots even hint at storage arrangements. Large jars remained downstairs in Building II; a line of small vessels may mark a shelf or bench. Heavy jars and upstairs storage were not always a happy combination.

Hasanlu yielded over 2,000 iron objects, including about 90 sickle blades and 90 small knives. Iron served harvesting and everyday cutting as well as warfare. Yet early iron was not automatically better than the finest bronze: consistent production of deliberately hardened steel is not established for this early transition.

At Nush-i Jan near Malayer, western Iran, plant remains include barley, wheat, peas, lentils and grapes. Some came from the sixth-century BCE community that reused the earlier monumental settlement. Handmade wide-mouthed cooking pots complement the food evidence. These finds illuminate real ingredients and equipment, even though no complete local cookbook survives.

Nush-i Jan’s main buildings, broadly dated about 750 to 550 BCE, include a temple with a raised fire altar and a hall supported by wooden columns. Builders used mud brick for towering walls and even curved vault supports. The site is conventionally discussed as Median; that does not identify every resident’s language or ancestry.

Two people discovered together at Hasanlu in 1973 became famous as “the lovers.” They died during the destruction around 800 BCE. Their close position suggests a human connection, but archaeology cannot decide whether they were partners, relatives, friends or strangers. A memorable nickname is not a recovered family record.

Their bones also offer a small glimpse of health: the younger adult had no observed dental disease or old healed injuries, while the older showed spinal changes including osteoarthritis. These are observations about two individuals, not a health survey or evidence for a particular treatment. Their stories preserve people as well as ruined buildings.

Hasanlu’s destruction around 800 BCE ended a particular settlement phase; its attackers are not securely identified. Sinai’s mining history and the Syrian kingdoms followed different paths. No single conquest, abandonment or disappearance explains everything included under this mixed atlas label.

ending.text: There was no single state here to fall in 500 BCE. Syrian kingdoms underwent separate Assyrian conquests, while Aramaic continued in Persian administration. The atlas endpoint marks neither a shared political collapse nor the disappearance of these regions’ inhabitants.
